Do two kernels imply the same distribution for the tips?

Source: R/equivalent.R
kernel_equivalent.Rd

Different evolutionary processes can imply exactly, or nearly, the same distribution for the species at the tips of a tree, and then no amount of extant data can tell them apart. On an ultrametric tree, for example, an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with a fixed root has the same kernel as an early-burst model with an accelerating rate r = 2 alpha.

Usage

kernel_equivalent(
  k1,
  k2,
  tree,
  pars = NULL,
  n_grid = 8,
  mean = c("free", "zero"),
  n_starts = 5,
  seed = 1
)

Arguments

k1

Kernel whose tip distribution is to be reproduced.

k2

Candidate kernel.

tree

A phylo tree (or the output of tree_info()).

pars

Optional parameter values of k1 (as in kernel_matrix()); by default a grid of n_grid settings spanning the bounds of its parameters.

n_grid

Number of parameter settings of k1 tried.

mean

"free" (unknown mean, contrasts only) or "zero".

n_starts

Number of starting points of the search over k2.

seed

Random seed for the starting points.

Value

A data frame (class phylogp_equivalence) with one row per setting of k1: its parameters, the smallest KL found, the best parameters of k2, and a verdict ("identical", "nearly identical" or "distinguishable").

Details

For each of several parameter settings of k1, kernel_equivalent() searches over all parameters of k2 (including the scales sigma) for the tip distribution closest to that of k1, measured by the Kullback-Leibler divergence $$KL = E_{k1}[\log p_{k1}(y) - \log p_{k2}(y)].$$ KL is the expected log-likelihood ratio in favour of k1 for one data set of these tips simulated from k1, when k2's parameters are chosen as well as possible. Values near 0 mean k2 can reproduce k1; values below about 1 mean the two will rarely be distinguishable with data of this size.

With mean = "free" (default), the trait mean is an unknown parameter, so only contrasts between species are compared, as in REML. Two kernels that differ only by a constant added to every covariance (such as a random versus a fixed root) are then equivalent. With mean = "zero" the full covariance matrices are compared.

The search is numerical, with several starting points. A small KL is therefore evidence of equivalence, but a large one means only that no equivalent parameter values were found.

Examples

tr <- ape::rcoal(30)
# OU with a fixed root vs accelerating early burst: identical on this tree
kernel_equivalent(k_ou(root = "fixed"), k_eb(upper = 20), tr, n_grid = 3)
#> Can eb() reproduce the tip distribution of ou(root = "fixed")?
#> 30 tips, ultrametric tree, unknown (contrasts compared) mean
#> 
#>  k1.ou1.sigma k1.ou1.alpha       KL k2.eb1.sigma k2.eb1.rate k2_at_bound
#>             1       0.0409 7.20e-10     9.51e-01      0.0819       FALSE
#>             1       1.2900 4.33e-09     2.06e-01      2.5900       FALSE
#>             1      40.9000 2.48e+00     3.27e-06     20.0000        TRUE
#>          verdict
#>        identical
#>        identical
#>  distinguishable
#> 
#> KL: expected log-likelihood ratio in favour of the first kernel for one
#> data set simulated from it, with the second kernel's parameters chosen as
#> well as possible.
#> In some settings the best parameters of the second kernel are at their bounds;
#> widen the bounds (e.g. k_eb(upper = )) before concluding that the kernels differ.
#> Equivalence depends on the parameter values of the first kernel.
